OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $k\geq 2$. Does\[(n+k)!^2 \mid (2n)!\]for infinitely many $n$?
#727: [EGRS75]
number theory | 
factorials
A conjecture of Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75]. It is open even for $k=2$.
Balakran [Ba29] proved this holds for $k=1$ - that is, $(n+1)^2\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for infinitely many $n$. It is a classical fact that $(n+1)\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for all $n$ (see Catalan numbers). 
Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus observe that the method of Balakran can be further used to prove that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[(n+k)!(n+1)! \mid (2n)!\](in fact this holds whenever $k<c \log n$ for some small constant $c>0$). 
Erdős [Er68c] proved that if $a!b!\mid n!$ then $a+b\leq n+O(\log n)$.

 The $k=2$ case is tantalizingly close to being within reach of current technology (in particular, the two-point logarithmically averaged Elliott and Chowla technology), which can provide a large number of $n$ with $n+1,n+2$ both somewhat smooth, which increases the odds of $(n+1)^2(n+2)^2$ dividing $\binom{2n}{n}$. Unfortunately the error terms in the current estimates are still somewhat weak (particularly in view of the relatively sparse nature of smooth numbers), and may not be enough to close this problem without additional effort.

 Thank you for this observation. I have a candidate unconditional proof for \(k=3\), hence also \(k=2\), using a different approach. The family \(n=210t^2+391t+179\) makes each of \(n+1,n+2,n+3\) factor into two linear forms; the argument exploits this structure through direct carry counting rather than Elliott–Chowla estimates.

 I've investigated a little whether the method in [728] can help here as well. It seems that it does allow you to handle up to moderately large primes, specifically if $n+1,\dots,n+k$ are $\exp(c \sqrt{\log n})$-smooth for some $c > 0$ it may work. Unfortunately, current techniques can only give consecutive integers that are roughly $n^\varepsilon$-smooth. Heuristically, one does expect the "$\exp(c \sqrt{\log n})$-smooth" to be true, but this seems far beyond current techniques. So probably [728] isn't helping all that much.

A partial proof 
claimed by Johan Land (using GPT-6-Astra, Fable 5.1, Gemini-3.8-Flash).
 Summary:
 I have a candidate PARTIAL unconditional proof for k=3 (which would also establish k=2). The construction 𝑛 =210⁢𝑡2 +391⁢𝑡 +179 makes each of 𝑛 +1,𝑛 +2,𝑛 +3 a product of two linear forms. A fixed progression handles small primes, while carry counting, uniform quadratic exponential-sum estimates, and a finite residue calculation control the remaining failures. The only external analytic input is the classical prime number theorem in fixed arithmetic progressions.
